Below is a structured overview of the development of UAE corporate law since 2012, focusing on the main federal statutes, key regulatory shifts, and the relatively limited but important body of case law. Because UAE corporate law is heavily statute- and regulation-driven, the “landmarks” are more often legislative reforms and ministerial/regulatory decisions than reported judicial precedents. Also, unlike common-law jurisdictions, onshore UAE court decisions are not comprehensively published, so the best-known “landmark cases” are often from the DIFC and ADGM common-law courts, or from publicly discussed constitutional/supreme court rulings.

I. Overview: the post-2012 trajectory

Since 2012, UAE corporate law has developed along five major lines:

1. Modernization of the federal companies regime, culminating in Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies.
2. Liberalization of foreign ownership, especially the removal of the long-standing 51% UAE national ownership rule for many onshore companies.
3. Strengthening of corporate governance, audit, disclosure, and beneficial ownership rules.
4. Integration with anti-money laundering, economic substance, and tax compliance frameworks.
5. Continued dual-track development between:
   - “onshore” UAE federal/company law; and
   - the financial free zones, especially the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) and Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), each with its own companies legislation and common-law courts.

II. The baseline before reform: Federal Law No. 8 of 1984

The principal pre-2015 statute was Federal Law No. 8 of 1984 Concerning Commercial Companies, as amended. It established the traditional company forms and the well-known rule that, for most onshore UAE limited liability companies, UAE nationals had to hold at least 51% of the share capital.

By 2012, this framework was widely viewed as outdated for a modern investment economy. Reform discussions accelerated after the global financial crisis and amid broader efforts to diversify the UAE economy.

III. First major modern reform: Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies

A. The statute

The first major landmark after 2012 was Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies (often called the “2015 CCL”), which repealed and replaced most of the 1984 law.

Full citation:
- Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies (United Arab Emirates).

It came into force on 1 July 2015, with transitional periods for existing companies.

B. Why it matters

The 2015 CCL was the foundational modern corporate statute for the UAE. It retained the traditional forms of companies but updated governance rules, minority protections, capital rules, and procedures for incorporation and administration.

Key features included:

1. Corporate forms clarified and modernized
   The law regulated:
   - general partnerships;
   - limited partnerships;
   - limited liability companies (LLCs);
   - private joint stock companies;
   - public joint stock companies (PJSCs);
   - simple commandite by shares and holding companies.

2. Governance reforms
   It introduced more detailed rules on:
   - directors’ duties and conflicts;
   - general assembly procedures;
   - related-party transactions;
   - auditor appointment and independence;
   - capital increases and reductions.

3. Removal of minimum capital for LLCs
   Instead of imposing a fixed federal minimum capital, the 2015 law generally required capital to be “sufficient to achieve the purpose of the company,” leaving greater flexibility to local licensing authorities.

4. Single-shareholder companies
   It expanded the ability to establish single-shareholder LLCs and PJSC-related structures in some contexts.

5. Public company regulation
   It strengthened the role of the Securities and Commodities Authority (SCA) in relation to PJSCs, governance, disclosure, and market conduct.

6. Continued foreign ownership restrictions
   Importantly, the 2015 CCL largely preserved the 51% UAE ownership requirement for most onshore companies, though with exceptions for GCC nationals, free zones, and strategic sectors.

C. Important implementing regulations and governance decisions

The 2015 CCL was supplemented by SCA governance regulations, including:

- Chairman of the SCA Board of Directors’ Decision No. 7/R.M of 2016 Concerning the Standards of Institutional Discipline and Governance of Public Joint Stock Companies.

This governance code was a significant milestone for listed and public companies, covering:
- board composition;
- independent directors;
- audit and nomination/remuneration committees;
- internal controls;
- governance reporting;
- conflict management.

IV. Specialized business and insolvency reforms that affected corporate law

Although not “company law” in the narrow sense, several statutes after 2015 materially changed the corporate legal environment.

A. Bankruptcy law

1. Federal Decree-Law No. 9 of 2016 on Bankruptcy
   Full citation:
   - Federal Decree-Law No. 9 of 2016 on Bankruptcy (United Arab Emirates).

This was a major development because it introduced a modern restructuring and insolvency framework for commercial companies and traders, including:
- preventive composition;
- restructuring procedures;
- bankruptcy liquidation;
- criminal and civil consequences for directors/managers in insolvency.

2. Federal Decree-Law No. 21 of 2020 amending the Bankruptcy Law
   This amendment was especially important during COVID-19, providing emergency support and procedural flexibility.

3. Federal Decree-Law No. 51 of 2023 on Financial Reorganisation and Bankruptcy
   Full citation:
   - Federal Decree-Law No. 51 of 2023 on Financial Reorganisation and Bankruptcy (United Arab Emirates).

This repealed and replaced much of the prior bankruptcy framework and is now the main insolvency statute affecting corporate distress and directors’ risk exposure.

B. Foreign direct investment

1. Federal Decree-Law No. 19 of 2018 on Foreign Direct Investment
   Full citation:
   - Federal Decree-Law No. 19 of 2018 on Foreign Direct Investment (United Arab Emirates).

This was a transitional landmark. It created the possibility of up to 100% foreign ownership in certain approved sectors and activities, subject to a “positive list” and local authority approvals.

Although later overtaken by broader reform, the 2018 FDI law was critical because it marked the beginning of the end of the blanket 51/49 ownership model.

C. Anti-money laundering and beneficial ownership

1. Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Financing of Illegal Organisations
   Full citation:
   - Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Financing of Illegal Organisations (United Arab Emirates).

This affected companies through:
- customer due diligence;
- recordkeeping;
- compliance systems;
- beneficial ownership transparency.

2. Cabinet Decision No. 58 of 2020 Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures
   Full citation:
   - Cabinet Decision No. 58 of 2020 Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures (United Arab Emirates).

This is a major corporate compliance milestone. It required many UAE companies to maintain:
- a register of ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs);
- a register of shareholders/partners;
- nominee director/shareholder disclosures.

3. Cabinet Decision No. 109 of 2023 Concerning the Regulation of Beneficial Owner Procedures
   This updated and replaced the 2020 regime, refining the compliance framework.

D. Economic substance

- Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 57 of 2020 concerning Economic Substance Requirements, together with Ministerial Decision No. 100 of 2020.

These rules, though tax/regulatory in nature, significantly affected holding companies, financing companies, headquarters entities, IP structures, and other UAE corporate vehicles.

E. Taxation and corporate structuring

1. Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 on the Taxation of Corporations and Businesses
   Full citation:
   - Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 on the Taxation of Corporations and Businesses (United Arab Emirates).

This is a watershed development. The introduction of federal corporate tax, effective for financial years beginning on or after 1 June 2023, changed:
- group structuring;
- holding company planning;
- transfer pricing compliance;
- governance and recordkeeping;
- free zone entity planning.

Though not a companies law statute, it has major implications for corporate law practice and governance.

V. The decisive break with the old model: 2020–2021 foreign ownership liberalization

A. Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2020 amending the 2015 Companies Law

Full citation:
- Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2020 Amending Certain Provisions of Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies (United Arab Emirates).

This was arguably the single most important corporate law reform of the decade before the 2021 restatement. It removed the default requirement that UAE nationals hold 51% of the share capital of onshore companies, except for activities deemed to have “strategic impact.”

This reform:
- enabled 100% foreign ownership for many mainland companies;
- shifted the old local shareholder model toward a licensing/sectoral approach;
- gave local emirate-level licensing authorities and the federal cabinet a larger role in determining strategic sectors.

B. Cabinet Decision No. 55 of 2021 on activities with strategic impact

Full citation:
- Cabinet Decision No. 55 of 2021 on Determining the List of Strategic Impact Activities (United Arab Emirates).

This decision identified sectors where ownership restrictions or enhanced regulation could still apply, such as:
- security and defense activities;
- banks, exchange houses, financing, and insurance;
- telecommunications;
- Hajj and Umrah services;
- fisheries-related activities;
- printing of the Holy Quran;
- certain commercial agency activities.

C. Practical significance

This reform fundamentally changed UAE corporate law and practice:
- foreign investors could directly own many mainland LLCs without nominee/local equity structures;
- M&A and joint venture documentation became simpler;
- constitutional documents and side agreements tied to local sponsorship became less central;
- due diligence increasingly focused on licensing restrictions rather than nationality percentages.

VI. Consolidation and modernization: Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies

A. The statute

Full citation:
- Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies (United Arab Emirates).

This is the current principal federal companies statute. It repealed Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 and came into force on 2 January 2022.

B. Why it is a landmark

The 2021 Companies Law consolidated the 2020 foreign ownership reforms and further modernized the UAE companies regime.

Key developments included:

1. 100% foreign ownership as the new general rule
   The law reflects the post-2020 position that companies may be wholly foreign-owned unless they engage in “strategic impact activities.”

2. More flexible governance for LLCs
   The 2021 law modernized:
   - quorum rules;
   - shareholder resolutions;
   - manager authorities;
   - share transfer rules;
   - pledges/security over shares;
   - dispute pathways.

3. Public company fundraising and listing
   It introduced greater flexibility for IPOs and public offerings, including allowing founders in some cases to sell a higher percentage in an IPO than under the older framework.

4. SPACs and modern capital market tools
   The post-2021 environment, together with SCA regulations, opened more room for structures such as special purpose acquisition companies and more flexible securities offerings.

5. ESG and governance pressure
   While not always explicit in the statute, the 2021 regime sits alongside stronger governance, disclosure, AML, and tax compliance expectations.

C. Implementing and related regulations

Important related regulatory instruments include:

- SCA Chairman Decision No. (3/R.M) of 2020 approving the Public Joint Stock Companies Governance Guide, later updated by subsequent SCA resolutions.
- SCA Decision No. 11/R.M of 2016 concerning the rules of mergers and acquisitions for public shareholding companies.
- Various Ministry of Economy and Department of Economic Development decisions at emirate level implementing foreign ownership changes.

VII. Other major corporate law developments since 2021

A. Family business legislation

- Federal Decree-Law No. 37 of 2022 concerning the Family Businesses (United Arab Emirates).

This is highly significant in the UAE context, where family-owned groups dominate much of the private sector. It provides a framework for:
- family business charters;
- governance arrangements;
- share transfer restrictions;
- continuity planning;
- dispute management.

B. Commercial agencies reform

- Federal Law No. 3 of 2022 Regulating Commercial Agencies (United Arab Emirates).

While not a general corporate law statute, it affects market entry structures, distributorships, and historical reliance on local agency models.

C. Competition law reform

- Federal Decree-Law No. 36 of 2023 on the Regulation of Competition (United Arab Emirates).

This affects mergers, acquisitions, and group structures and is increasingly relevant to corporate transactions.

VIII. Landmark cases

A. General caution on UAE case law

For onshore UAE corporate law, there is no equivalent of a fully indexed, routinely cited body of precedent as in England or other common-law systems. Many important rulings of the UAE Federal Supreme Court and the Dubai and Abu Dhabi Courts of Cassation are not easily accessible in official English translation. As a result, “landmark cases” are harder to identify with precision than “landmark statutes.”

Still, several categories of cases matter:

1. constitutional/federal supreme court rulings on the division of legislative power or company-related questions;
2. cassation-level cases on manager/director liability, share transfers, arbitration clauses, and corporate authority;
3. DIFC and ADGM cases, which are more accessible and precedential within their own systems.

B. Onshore themes in case law

The most important recurring onshore case-law themes since 2012 have been:

1. Separate legal personality
   UAE courts have generally respected company separateness, but they may scrutinize sham arrangements, nominee structures, and abuse of authority.

2. Manager and director authority
   Cassation cases frequently address whether a manager had authority to bind the company, especially where constitutional documents, powers of attorney, or licensing records limit authority.

3. Side agreements and nominee shareholding
   Before 100% foreign ownership reform, many disputes concerned side agreements intended to alter the economic effect of the 51/49 ownership rule. Courts often approached such arrangements cautiously where they conflicted with mandatory law or public policy.

4. Arbitration clauses in constitutional documents and shareholder disputes
   UAE courts have considered whether arbitration clauses bind companies, shareholders, managers, and successors, particularly where the clause appears in articles of association or related agreements.

Because many of these decisions are not consistently reported, practitioners often rely more on statutory text and local procedural practice than on published precedent.

C. DIFC cases with broader corporate significance

Although DIFC law is separate from onshore federal company law, DIFC cases have had real significance for UAE corporate practice, especially in shareholder disputes, directors’ duties, and interim remedies.

1. Pearl Petroleum Co Ltd v Kurdistan Regional Government of Iraq
   There are several decisions in this long-running DIFC litigation and enforcement saga. One often-cited decision is:
   - Pearl Petroleum Company Limited v The Kurdistan Regional Government of Iraq [2017] DIFC CFI 027.

While not a pure UAE companies law case, it is significant for:
- shareholder and joint venture structuring;
- enforcement strategy through UAE financial free zone courts;
- recognition of arbitration-connected corporate rights.

2. Nest Investments Holding Lebanon SAL v Deloitte & Touche (ME)
   - Nest Investments Holding Lebanon SAL v Deloitte & Touche (ME) [2018] DIFC CA 011.

This case is often discussed in relation to:
- reflective loss;
- shareholder claims versus company claims;
- limits on investor recovery for losses suffered through a company.

That theme is highly relevant to corporate litigation across the UAE.

   - Bank Sarasin-Alpen (ME) Ltd v Ahmed Hamad Algosaibi & Brothers Co; and related DIFC proceedings.
   - There are also connected appellate decisions involving Al Khorafi interests.

These cases are important for:
- corporate authority;
- agency;
- financial services liability;
- jurisdictional interaction between DIFC and onshore courts.

The relationship between DIFC courts and onshore Dubai courts generated important jurisprudence affecting corporate litigation strategy.

Examples include cases involving the Dubai Courts–DIFC Courts Joint Judicial Committee established by:
- Decree No. 19 of 2016 Establishing a Judicial Tribunal for the Dubai Courts and the DIFC Courts.

Cases before that tribunal, while not “company law” in the narrow sense, materially affected:
- forum selection;
- enforcement of judgments and arbitral awards;
- tactical use of DIFC proceedings in shareholder and commercial disputes.

E. ADGM developments

ADGM has developed its own companies and insolvency case law under a common-law model, but its jurisprudence is still less extensive than that of the DIFC. Its significance lies more in legislative innovation than in a large body of landmark cases.

IX. DIFC and ADGM statutory developments as parallel corporate law landmarks

A. DIFC

1. DIFC Companies Law No. 5 of 2018
   Full citation:
   - Dubai International Financial Centre Law No. 5 of 2018, Companies Law.

2. DIFC Operating Law No. 7 of 2018
   Full citation:
   - Dubai International Financial Centre Law No. 7 of 2018, Operating Law.

3. DIFC Foundations Law No. 3 of 2018
   Full citation:
   - Dubai International Financial Centre Law No. 3 of 2018, Foundations Law.

These laws modernized:
- incorporation and administration;
- directors’ duties;
- shareholder rights;
- beneficial ownership and registrar requirements;
- corporate structuring tools for family offices and holding structures.

ADGM’s framework is heavily based on English company law concepts. Key instruments include:
- ADGM Companies Regulations 2020.
- ADGM Commercial Licensing Regulations.
- ADGM Insolvency Regulations 2022.

ADGM has become important for:
- holding companies;
- SPVs;
- foundations;
- family wealth structures;
- venture capital and fund-related structures.

The most important legal shifts can be summarized as follows:

1. From nationality-based ownership rules to activity-based regulation
   The old 51/49 rule was the defining feature of UAE company law for decades. Since 2020–2021, the focus has shifted to whether an activity is “strategic.”

2. From formal incorporation rules to governance and compliance
   The legal burden on companies increasingly lies in:
   - governance;
   - AML/UBO compliance;
   - sanctions screening;
   - accounting;
   - tax and transfer pricing;
   - substance and reporting.

3. From domestic company law to integrated regulatory corporate law
   UAE corporate law now operates in conjunction with:
   - securities regulation;
   - insolvency law;
   - competition law;
   - tax law;
   - AML law;
   - beneficial ownership disclosure.

4. Continued pluralism of legal systems
   Corporate law in the UAE remains multi-layered:
   - federal onshore law;
   - emirate-level licensing rules;
   - DIFC law;
   - ADGM law;
   - sector-specific regulation for banks, insurers, telecoms, and state-linked entities.

If the question is asked in a comparative-law sense, the honest answer is that UAE corporate law since 2012 has been shaped far more by statutes and regulatory decisions than by a stable canon of publicly reported onshore corporate cases.

Still, the most practically significant case clusters are:

1. Onshore cassation and supreme court decisions on:
   - manager authority;
   - validity of share transfers;

2. DIFC Court of Appeal and Court of First Instance cases on:
   - shareholder loss and reflective loss:

   - enforcement and corporate/joint venture disputes:
     - Pearl Petroleum Company Limited v The Kurdistan Regional Government of Iraq [2017] DIFC CFI 027.
   - jurisdiction and enforcement conflicts via the Judicial Tribunal under Dubai Decree No. 19 of 2016.

XIII. Conclusion

Since 2012, UAE corporate law has moved from a relatively rigid, ownership-restrictive, formalistic regime to a more open, internationally aligned, compliance-intensive system.

The central milestones are:

- the replacement of the old 1984 law by Federal Law No. 2 of 2015;
- the dismantling of the 51% local ownership rule through Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2020;
- the consolidation of the new framework in Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021;

## 1. Core statutory development since 2021

## A. Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies
The central development is:

- **Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies** (UAE), issued 20 September 2021, effective 2 January 2022.

This law replaced the prior principal companies legislation:

- **Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies**.

### Why it is landmark
Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 is the key modernizing statute for UAE onshore corporate law. It consolidated reforms already underway and aligned company law with the UAE’s broader investment strategy.

### Major changes
Among the most important reforms:

#### 1. Full or near-full foreign ownership
This was linked to the earlier reform:
- **Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2020 amending certain provisions of Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies**.

That 2020 decree removed the general requirement that UAE nationals hold 51% of onshore companies, subject to “strategic impact” activities. The 2021 Companies Law carried this liberalized regime forward.

**Impact:**  
This is arguably the single most transformative shift in UAE corporate law in recent decades. It changed the default ownership structure for limited liability companies (“LLCs”) and public/private joint stock companies outside the free zones.

#### 2. Simplified LLC governance
The 2021 law modernized rules for:
- incorporation;
- shareholder resolutions;
- managers’ powers;
- capital structure; and
- governance flexibility.

It made the LLC more usable as the standard business vehicle for domestic and foreign investors.

#### 3. SPACs, IPOs, and capital markets alignment
The law and related securities regulations facilitated:
- special purpose acquisition companies;
- dual-class and modern financing structures in some contexts;
- improved public offering frameworks;
- closer alignment with **Securities and Commodities Authority (“SCA”)** rules.

#### 4. Directors’ and managers’ duties
The law sharpened rules on:
- conflict of interest;
- related-party transactions;
- liability for mismanagement;
- shareholder action against directors/managers.

#### 5. Corporate governance for PJSCs
Public joint stock companies became subject to more detailed governance obligations, reinforced by SCA rulemaking.

A second major stream of reform concerns ownership transparency.

The key instrument is:
- **Cabinet Decision No. 58 of 2020 Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures**, as amended and implemented through subsequent regulatory guidance and local registrar practice after 2021.

Although enacted in 2020, it became operationally central from 2021 onward as registries and licensing authorities enforced:
- UBO registers;
- nominee director/shareholder disclosure;
- compliance filing obligations.

### 2. AML/CFT linkage
Corporate law has increasingly intersected with anti-money laundering law, especially under:
- **Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Financing of Illegal Organisations**, as amended;
- implementing regulations and guidance from the Ministry of Economy, Central Bank, and Executive Office for AML/CFT.

**Corporate significance:**  
Companies must now treat ownership transparency, internal controls, and recordkeeping as core governance matters, not merely licensing formalities.

## C. Insolvency and restructuring reform affecting corporate practice

- **Federal Decree-Law No. 51 of 2023 on Financial Restructuring and Bankruptcy**.

- **Federal Decree-Law No. 9 of 2016 on Bankruptcy**, as amended.

### Why it matters for corporate law
Although formally insolvency legislation, it deeply affects:
- directors’ duties in financial distress;
- creditor/shareholder relations;
- rescue financing;
- corporate group restructuring;
- continuity of business operations.

The 2023 law is generally seen as making restructuring more accessible and more commercially realistic, while trying to reduce stigma and procedural friction.

### Corporate-law significance
It influences the governance of companies nearing insolvency, especially around:
- wrongful trading-type concerns;
- preservation of assets;
- management accountability;
- court-supervised restructuring.

---

## D. Free-zone corporate law modernization

The UAE corporate landscape cannot be understood without the DIFC and ADGM.

### 1. DIFC developments
The DIFC already had a developed company-law framework under:
- **DIFC Companies Law, DIFC Law No. 5 of 2018**;
- **DIFC Operating Law, DIFC Law No. 7 of 2018**;
- **DIFC Insolvency Law, DIFC Law No. 1 of 2019**.

Since 2021, the significance lies less in wholesale replacement and more in:
- continued refinement through regulations;
- judicial interpretation by the DIFC Courts;
- stronger enforcement culture around governance, shareholder remedies, and insolvency.

### 2. ADGM developments
ADGM’s corporate regime, based heavily on English common law and regulations, continued to mature after 2021 through:
- amendments to the **Companies Regulations 2020**;
- insolvency and restructuring practice under ADGM regulations;
- common-law judicial decisions on shareholder disputes, fiduciary duties, and jurisdiction.

### Why free-zone developments matter
DIFC and ADGM often serve as laboratories for advanced corporate law concepts:
- derivative actions;
- unfair prejudice-style shareholder remedies;
- sophisticated insolvency tools;
- governance standards familiar to international investors.

These regimes influence expectations and practice even in onshore UAE transactions.

---

## E. Competition, tax, and economic substance as part of the corporate-law environment

Strictly speaking, these are not all “company law” statutes, but they have reshaped corporate structuring since 2021.

### 1. Corporate tax
The introduction of federal corporate taxation is transformative:
- **Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 on the Taxation of Corporations and Businesses**.

Effective for financial years beginning on or after 1 June 2023, it changed:
- group structuring;
- holding company arrangements;
- transfer pricing governance;
- board-level compliance responsibilities.

### 2. Competition law
- **Federal Decree-Law No. 36 of 2023 Regulating Competition**.

This matters for M&A, group reorganizations, and joint ventures.

### 3. Economic substance and business structuring
The economic substance regime, though introduced earlier, continued to shape governance and documentation after 2021, especially where companies claimed tax or treaty advantages.

---

## 2. Important themes in case law

A caution: UAE onshore precedent is not binding in the common-law sense, and official publication is uneven. For that reason, “landmark cases” in UAE corporate law are more readily identified in the DIFC and ADGM, where judgments are published and reasoned in detail.

## A. DIFC cases on shareholder rights, governance, and jurisdiction

### 1. The broader Banyan Tree / conduit jurisdiction line
A significant DIFC Courts development affecting corporate disputes is the recognition and enforcement architecture associated with:
- **Banyan Tree Corporate Pte Ltd v Meydan Group LLC** [2013] DIFC CA 005 (Dubai DIFC Court of Appeal).

Although pre-2021, its influence continued strongly after 2021. It established the DIFC Courts’ role in enforcement and “conduit” jurisdiction, which has major implications for:
- enforcement of shareholder awards;
- corporate debt claims;
- cross-border corporate disputes.

Post-2021, this line remains important because corporate litigants continue to use DIFC mechanisms strategically.

### 2. Taaleem and other governance-related DIFC disputes
A number of post-2021 DIFC cases have concerned:
- contractual governance rights;
- shareholder agreements;
- board authority;
- interim relief;
- enforcement of arbitral awards in corporate settings.

The precise “landmark” status of these decisions is often practical rather than doctrinal: they demonstrate the DIFC Courts’ willingness to grant sophisticated commercial remedies.

### 3. Insolvency cases in the DIFC
The DIFC Courts have continued to develop restructuring and insolvency jurisprudence under the DIFC Insolvency Law 2019, including issues relating to:
- officeholders’ powers;
- recognition;
- creditor priorities;
- restructuring supervision.

These cases matter for directors and shareholders because they clarify the shift from equity governance to creditor protection in distress.

---

## B. ADGM cases
ADGM judgments since 2021 have reinforced:
- application of common-law fiduciary principles;
- court support for restructuring and insolvency;
- high standards for corporate recordkeeping and governance.

ADGM’s significance lies in the availability of detailed judgments and a legal environment familiar to international investors. However, compared with the DIFC, the volume of reported corporate cases is still smaller.

---

## C. Onshore UAE court themes

Onshore judgments since 2021 have tended to address recurring issues such as:

### 1. Validity of shareholder resolutions
Courts have continued to scrutinize:
- notice requirements;
- quorum;
- authority of signatories;
- amendment of memoranda/articles;
- manager authority in LLCs.

### 2. Manager/director liability
There has been continued litigation over:
- misuse of company funds;
- acting beyond authority;
- conflicts of interest;
- failure to maintain records;
- civil and, in some cases, criminal exposure.

### 3. Arbitration clauses in corporate documents
A recurring issue is whether disputes concerning:
- share transfers;
- shareholder agreements;
- corporate resolutions;
- manager appointments  
must go to arbitration or to local courts.

### 4. Company dissolution and deadlock
The courts continue to be asked to dissolve LLCs and appoint experts where:
- relations between shareholders break down;
- there is oppression or exclusion;
- the company’s purpose becomes impracticable.

Because many of these decisions are not consistently reported in accessible official series, they are better understood as doctrinal trends than as universally cited “leading cases.”

---

## 3. Landmark statutes since 2021

If the question is which statutes are truly “landmark,” the list is relatively clear.

## 1. Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies
**Most important corporate-law statute since 2021.**

Key reasons:
- carried forward foreign ownership liberalization;
- modernized LLC and PJSC governance;
- improved capital markets compatibility;
- updated directors’ and managers’ duties.

## 2. Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 on the Taxation of Corporations and Businesses
Not a company law statute in the narrow sense, but a landmark for corporate structuring and governance.

## 3. Federal Decree-Law No. 51 of 2023 on Financial Restructuring and Bankruptcy
Landmark for distressed companies, restructurings, and director conduct in the vicinity of insolvency.

## 4. Federal Decree-Law No. 36 of 2023 Regulating Competition
Important for M&A and group organization.

## 5. UBO / transparency framework
- **Cabinet Decision No. 58 of 2020 Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures**  
and post-2021 enforcement practice.

This is landmark in practical compliance terms.

## 6. SCA governance and market regulations
For listed companies, important reforms also came through SCA rulebooks and decisions, especially on:
- governance;
- related-party transactions;
- public offerings;
- market conduct.

Depending on the exact instrument and year, these can be highly significant even if less famous than the Companies Law itself.

---

## 4. Landmark cases: what can fairly be called “landmark”?

Because UAE corporate law is statute-centered and case reporting is uneven, the best answer is to distinguish between:

- **truly landmark reported cases** mostly from the DIFC/ADGM; and
- **important onshore trends** rather than single canonical cases.

### A. Cases that remain influential in the post-2021 period
Even if some predate 2021, they still shape the law’s development after 2021:

1. **Banyan Tree Corporate Pte Ltd v Meydan Group LLC** [2013] DIFC CA 005, DIFC Court of Appeal  
   - important for jurisdiction/enforcement architecture affecting corporate disputes.

2. DIFC insolvency and restructuring cases under the **DIFC Insolvency Law No. 1 of 2019**  
   - these continue to define the treatment of distressed companies and directors.

3. ADGM cases applying common-law fiduciary and corporate governance principles  
   - important for persuasive development, especially in shareholder disputes.

### B. Onshore “landmark” areas rather than named cases
Since 2021, the most important judicial developments onshore concern:
- shareholder meeting validity;
- authority of LLC managers;
- misuse of powers;
- nullification of resolutions;
- dissolution for deadlock;
- expert-driven accounting and valuation disputes.

In practice, many leading practitioners rely more on:
- text of **Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021**;
- implementing regulations;
- registry practice;
- SCA guidance;
- and unpublished or subscription-reported judgments  
than on a stable canon of publicly available “leading cases.”

---

# Overall assessment: the development of UAE corporate law since 2021

The trajectory since 2021 can be summarized in five points:

## 1. Liberalization
The UAE decisively moved away from mandatory majority-UAE ownership in most sectors, making onshore incorporation more attractive to foreign investors.

## 2. Modernization
The 2021 Companies Law modernized governance, especially for LLCs and PJSCs.

## 3. Transparency
UBO, AML, and compliance obligations became central to corporate administration.

## 4. Institutional diversification
DIFC and ADGM continued to supply sophisticated common-law corporate adjudication, while onshore law remained codified and commercially pragmatic.

## 5. Integration with tax, insolvency, and competition law
Corporate law can no longer be viewed in isolation. Since 2021, tax, restructuring, and competition rules have become part of the core legal architecture for UAE companies.

---

# Short answer: the main landmark statutes

If you want the shortest possible list of landmark statutes since 2021, it is:

1. **Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies**  
2. **Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 on the Taxation of Corporations and Businesses**  
3. **Federal Decree-Law No. 51 of 2023 on Financial Restructuring and Bankruptcy**  
4. **Federal Decree-Law No. 36 of 2023 Regulating Competition**  
5. **Cabinet Decision No. 58 of 2020 Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures** as enforced post-2021

And for case law, the most genuinely citable “landmark” reported decisions are still concentrated in the **DIFC** and **ADGM**, rather than in the onshore federal courts.

If you want, I can turn this into:
1. a **chronological timeline from 2021 to 2025**, or  
2. a **table of statutes and cases with one-line significance notes**, or  
3. a **jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction breakdown: onshore UAE vs DIFC vs ADGM**.

Below is a structured overview of the **development of criminal law in England and Wales since 2006**, focusing on the most important **statutes**, **landmark appellate decisions**, and major **institutional / procedural reforms**. Because “criminal law” is very broad, I have organised it by theme and chronology.

---

# 1. Overview: the main trends since 2006

Since 2006, criminal law in England and Wales has developed along several clear lines:

1. **Expansion and modernisation of substantive offences**
   - especially in relation to **sexual offences**, **terrorism**, **fraud**, **modern slavery**, **cyber-enabled abuse**, and **coercive control**.

2. **Greater emphasis on public protection and risk management**
   - through sentencing reforms, dangerous offender provisions, sexual harm orders, terrorism prevention measures, and stronger victim-protection mechanisms.

3. **A stronger victims’ rights framework**
   - especially in domestic abuse, sexual offending, stalking, and trafficking.

4. **Human-rights-inflected criminal adjudication**
   - with the courts repeatedly addressing compatibility with the **European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)** under the **Human Rights Act 1998**, especially on hearsay, joint enterprise, whole life orders, privacy, and fair trial rights.

5. **Major appellate correction of doctrine**
   - the clearest example being the Supreme Court’s reformulation of **joint enterprise** in **R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8; [2017] AC 387**.

6. **Continuing procedural and evidential reform**
   - including bad character, hearsay, disclosure, sentencing guidelines, and the growing use of special measures and remote evidence.

---

# 2. Key statutes since 2006

## A. Fraud and economic crime

### Fraud Act 2006
**Fraud Act 2006**, in force largely from 15 January 2007, was one of the most important substantive criminal law reforms of the period.

It replaced the old deception offences with a general offence of **fraud** under three routes:
- **fraud by false representation** (s 2),
- **fraud by failing to disclose information** (s 3),
- **fraud by abuse of position** (s 4).

It also created:
- **possession of articles for use in frauds** (s 6),
- **making or supplying articles for use in frauds** (s 7),
- **obtaining services dishonestly** (s 11).

This was a major doctrinal shift away from the technical and fragmented deception offences under the **Theft Acts**.

### Bribery Act 2010
The **Bribery Act 2010** modernised corruption law and is one of the most significant criminal statutes of the era. It created:
- bribing another person (s 1),
- being bribed (s 2),
- bribery of foreign public officials (s 6),
- the corporate offence of **failure of commercial organisations to prevent bribery** (s 7).

The s 7 “failure to prevent” model later influenced economic crime reform more generally.

### Criminal Finances Act 2017
The **Criminal Finances Act 2017** strengthened the anti-money laundering and proceeds-of-crime regime, including:
- **Unexplained Wealth Orders**,
- new powers concerning seizure and forfeiture,
- corporate offences of **failure to prevent facilitation of tax evasion**.

### Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act 2022
This Act, passed rapidly in the context of sanctions and illicit finance concerns, strengthened sanctions enforcement and beneficial ownership transparency.

### Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023
A major recent development. Among other things, it:
- reformed the identification doctrine for corporate criminal liability,
- expanded the **failure to prevent fraud** offence framework,
- strengthened Companies House and anti-economic-crime mechanisms.

This statute is central to the contemporary development of corporate criminal law.

---

## B. Violent crime, weapons, and public protection

### Violent Crime Reduction Act 2006
The **Violent Crime Reduction Act 2006** introduced measures on firearms, knives, alcohol-related disorder, and age restrictions. It formed part of the broader “public protection” legislative agenda of the mid-2000s.

### Corporate Manslaughter and Corporate Homicide Act 2007
This Act was a landmark in homicide law. It created the offence of:
- **corporate manslaughter** in England and Wales (s 1).

It addressed longstanding difficulties with attributing gross negligence manslaughter to large companies under the old identification doctrine.

### Offensive weapons legislation
Important later measures include:
- **Offensive Weapons Act 2019**, addressing knife crime, corrosive substances, and certain prohibited weapons;
- related amendments to possession and sale offences.

### Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022
A very wide-ranging Act. In criminal law terms it:
- increased some maximum penalties,
- created and expanded public order and protest-related powers,
- changed sentencing and release arrangements,
- addressed unauthorised encampments and other public-order-related matters.

### Public Order Act 2023
This Act further expanded protest-related criminal offences and police powers, including offences linked to locking-on and interference with key infrastructure. It is one of the most controversial recent criminal statutes on civil liberties grounds.

---

## C. Sexual offences, domestic abuse, and protection from interpersonal abuse

### Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
Among many other things, this Act created the offence of:
- **possession of extreme pornographic images** (s 63).

### Sexual Offences Act 2003 developments
Although the **Sexual Offences Act 2003** predates 2006, much post-2006 criminal law development has involved interpretation and amendment of that Act, especially around:
- consent,
- child sexual offences,
- sexual harm prevention orders,
- notification requirements.

### Protection of Freedoms Act 2012
This Act made significant changes including:
- reform of **sexual offences prevention orders** and related civil preventive orders,
- changes to the **DNA and fingerprint retention** regime in response to Strasbourg jurisprudence,
- creation of new offences such as **stalking** by amendments to the **Protection from Harassment Act 1997**.

On stalking, it inserted:
- **s 2A**: stalking,
- **s 4A**: stalking involving fear of violence or serious alarm or distress.

### Serious Crime Act 2015
A major modern statute. It created, among other things:
- the offence of **controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship** (s 76),
- offences relating to **female genital mutilation** and child cruelty reforms,
- new **sexual communication with a child** offence was later created by the **Sexual Offences Act 2003**, inserted by the **Serious Crime Act 2015** (s 67).

The coercive control offence marked a profound conceptual shift: criminal law moved beyond isolated incidents of violence to patterns of domination and abuse.

### Voyeurism (Offences) Act 2019
This Act created the so-called **upskirting** offence by amending the **Sexual Offences Act 2003**.

### Domestic Abuse Act 2021
One of the most important recent statutes. It:
- created a statutory definition of **domestic abuse** (s 1),
- recognised **economic abuse**,
- strengthened protective orders,
- prohibited cross-examination in person in family and civil proceedings in certain circumstances,
- created the offence of **non-fatal strangulation or suffocation** (s 70, inserting s 75A into the **Serious Crime Act 2015**),
- widened the **controlling or coercive behaviour** offence beyond co-residential relationships.

This Act is a landmark in the criminal law’s recognition of the dynamics of abuse.

### Online Safety Act 2023
Although broader than criminal law, it introduced or reshaped important criminal offences relating to online harms, including cyberflashing and communications offences.

---

## D. Terrorism and national security

### Terrorism Act 2006
Although enacted in 2006, it set the tone for the period, creating offences including:
- encouragement of terrorism (s 1),
- dissemination of terrorist publications (s 2),
- preparation of terrorist acts (s 5).

### Counter-Terrorism Act 2008
This expanded powers relating to post-charge questioning, asset freezing, and information gathering.

### Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures Act 2011
This replaced control orders with **TPIMs**, a major development in preventive national security law.

### Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015
Introduced measures including:
- temporary exclusion orders,
- seizure of passports,
- the **Prevent duty** on specified authorities.

### Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019
This created and expanded offences including:
- entering or remaining in a designated area overseas,
- viewing terrorist material online in certain circumstances,
- stronger border and publication-related powers.

Terrorism law since 2006 has been characterised by preventive, anticipatory criminalisation and repeated human-rights challenges.

---

## E. Human trafficking, slavery, and immigration crime

### Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004
Predates 2006, but remained relevant in trafficking and document offences.

### Modern Slavery Act 2015
A major landmark. It consolidated and strengthened offences of:
- slavery, servitude and forced or compulsory labour (s 1),
- human trafficking (s 2).

It also introduced:
- the office of the **Independent Anti-slavery Commissioner**,
- slavery and trafficking prevention/risk orders,
- a statutory defence for some victims compelled to offend (s 45).

This was one of the most important criminal justice statutes of the decade.

### Nationality and Borders Act 2022
Among other things, it altered aspects of trafficking and immigration-related criminal law and has been controversial for its impact on victim protection.

### Illegal Migration Act 2023
Though much of its significance is public law and immigration law, it also bears on the practical operation of trafficking protections and criminal justice responses.

---

## F. Sentencing and criminal justice system reform

### Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
Important for sentencing, prison and public protection.

### Coroners and Justice Act 2009
A major Act. In criminal law, it:
- reformed **partial defences to murder**:
  - replacing provocation with **loss of control** (ss 54–56),
- created the offence of **causing death by careless or inconsiderate driving**,
- abolished the common law offence of sedition and seditious libel,
- addressed revenge pornography precursors only indirectly, but was important in communications/privacy contexts.

The homicide reforms are among the most important substantive criminal law changes of the period.

### Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012
Important for legal aid and sentencing framework changes.

### Crime and Courts Act 2013
Created the **deferred prosecution agreement** regime for certain economic crimes.

### Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015
Included changes to criminal courts and procedure.

### Sentencing Act 2020
This consolidated a large body of sentencing legislation. It is doctrinally important because sentencing law had become highly fragmented. It did not radically change sentencing principles by itself, but it made the law more accessible and coherent.

### Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022
Again important here for:
- whole life order changes,
- release and sentencing changes,
- serious violence reduction and public-order powers.

---

# 3. Landmark cases since 2006

## A. Joint enterprise: the most significant doctrinal correction

### R v Jogee
**R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8; [2017] AC 387, Supreme Court**

This is arguably the single most important criminal law case since 2006.

The Supreme Court held that the law had taken a “wrong turn” in treating **foresight** that the principal might commit the crime as sufficient for secondary liability. Foresight is evidence of intent, but **not the legal test itself**. The accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal offence.

This overruled the prior understanding associated with:
- **Chan Wing-Siu v The Queen [1985] AC 168 (PC)**,
- **R v Powell; R v English [1999] 1 AC 1 (HL)**.

**Impact:** profound. It reshaped murder prosecutions, gang cases, and appellate litigation on unsafe convictions.

### R v Johnson and others
**R v Johnson; R v Farooq; R v Crilly [2016] EWCA Crim 1613**

The Court of Appeal addressed appeals following **Jogee**, making clear that not every pre-Jogee conviction was automatically unsafe; the appellant had to show substantial injustice.

---

## B. Loss of control and homicide reform

### R v Clinton; R v Parker; R v Evans
**[2012] EWCA Crim 2; [2013] QB 1, Court of Appeal**

A leading case on the **loss of control** defence under **Coroners and Justice Act 2009, ss 54–55**. The court held that sexual infidelity could not on its own constitute a qualifying trigger, but could be considered as part of the factual context where other qualifying triggers existed.

This is the leading authority on the interpretation of the post-2009 partial defence.

### R v Dawes
**R v Dawes [2013] EWCA Crim 322; [2013] 1 WLR 3156**

Clarified aspects of:
- the “fear of serious violence” trigger,
- the “things said or done” trigger,
- the exclusion where the defendant incited the violence.

### R v Jewell
**R v Jewell [2014] EWCA Crim 414**

Further authority on the objective element of loss of control.

---

## C. Consent in sexual offences

### R (F) v DPP
**R (F) v Director of Public Prosecutions [2013] EWHC 945 (Admin); [2014] QB 581**

Concerned deception and consent under the **Sexual Offences Act 2003**. The courts have continued to develop the distinction between deceptions that negate consent under ss 74–76 and those that do not.

### Assange v Swedish Prosecution Authority
**Assange v Swedish Prosecution Authority [2011] EWHC 2849 (Admin); [2012] UKSC 22; [2012] 2 AC 471**

Not principally a criminal law doctrine case, but significant for sexual offence allegations and extradition procedure.

### R v Lawrance
**R v Lawrance [2020] UKSC 2; [2020] AC 245, Supreme Court**

Clarified the meaning of consent under **s 74 Sexual Offences Act 2003**. The defendant had deceived the complainant as to his fertility status. The Supreme Court held that deception of this kind did not automatically vitiate consent for the purposes of rape under s 1, drawing careful boundaries around when deception negates “choice”.

### R v McNally
**R v McNally [2013] EWCA Crim 1051; [2014] QB 593**

The Court of Appeal held that deception as to gender could vitiate consent under s 74. This was a controversial and significant development in sexual offences law.

### R v B
**R v B [2013] EWCA Crim 823**

Important on conditional consent and deception.

### R v Kaitamaki; R (Monica) line
More recent civil/criminal crossover litigation has also influenced understanding of autonomy, privacy, and sexual wrongdoing, though not always by creating criminal doctrine directly.

---

## D. Extreme intoxication and criminal responsibility

### R v Kingston
Earlier authority remained important, but the modern development is:

### R v Taj
**R v Taj [2018] EWCA Crim 1743**

Illustrated continuing application of intoxication principles.

### R v Hardie
Earlier authority remained relevant.

### R v Heard
**R v Heard [2007] EWCA Crim 125; [2008] QB 43**

Important on the distinction between crimes of basic and specific intent in intoxication law.

### DPP v Beard
Historic authority remains foundational.

### R v Grant
**R v Grant [2024] UKSC 29**  
This is a very important recent Supreme Court decision on **automatism / extreme self-induced intoxication** and the compatibility of the common law rule in **R v Majewski [1977] AC 443 (HL)** with principle and statute. It confirms the continuing significance of Majewski while clarifying the doctrinal basis of intoxication liability.

---

## E. Self-defence and householders’ force

### Crime and Courts Act 2013
Inserted special provisions on householders’ cases into the **Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s 76** framework.

### R (Collins) v Secretary of State for Justice
**R (Collins) v Secretary of State for Justice [2016] EWHC 33 (Admin); [2016] 1 WLR 2534**

Considered the compatibility and interpretation of the “householder defence” standard permitting force that is not grossly disproportionate.

### R v Ray
**R v Ray [2017] EWCA Crim 1391**

An important appellate authority on self-defence directions and s 76.

---

## F. Hearsay, confrontation, and fair trial

### Horncastle
**R v Horncastle [2009] UKSC 14; [2010] 2 AC 373**

A major Supreme Court case on hearsay under the **Criminal Justice Act 2003** and **Article 6 ECHR**. The Court declined to follow Strasbourg uncritically and held that the English hearsay regime could be Convention-compliant even where a conviction was based significantly on absent-witness evidence, depending on safeguards.

This is one of the leading criminal evidence cases of the period.

### Al-Khawaja and Tahery v United Kingdom
**Al-Khawaja and Tahery v United Kingdom (2011) 54 EHRR 23, ECtHR (GC)**

Not a domestic case, but essential to understanding the development of hearsay law and confrontation rights. It influenced later domestic case law.

### R v Ibrahim; R v Boutros
**[2012] EWCA Crim 837**

Further development of hearsay and Article 6 principles post-Horncastle.

---

## G. Bad character and sexual history evidence

### R v Hanson
**R v Hanson; R v Gilmore; R v Pickstone [2005] EWCA Crim 824; [2005] 1 WLR 3169**
Predates 2006 but remained foundational for bad character law under the **Criminal Justice Act 2003** throughout the period.

### R v T
**R v T [2020] EWCA Crim 1470**

Important in the continuing interpretation of bad character and propensity.

### R v Evans
**R v Evans [2016] EWCA Crim 452**
A leading case on the admissibility of complainants’ sexual behaviour evidence under **Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999, s 41**, especially where necessary for fairness.

---

## H. Murder, unlawful act manslaughter, and causation

### R v Gnango
**R v Gnango [2011] UKSC 59; [2012] 1 AC 827**

A controversial Supreme Court decision. In a gunfight case, the defendant was held liable for murder when a bystander was killed by the other shooter. The case is important for transferred malice, joint enterprise-related reasoning, and causation.

### R v Golds
**R v Golds [2016] UKSC 61; [2017] AC 387**

A major Supreme Court authority on diminished responsibility under **Homicide Act 1957, s 2** as amended by the **Coroners and Justice Act 2009**. It clarified the meaning of an “abnormality of mental functioning” that provides an explanation for the killing and the requirement that it substantially impair the defendant’s ability.

### R v Hughes
**R v Hughes [2013] UKSC 56; [2013] 1 WLR 2461**

A leading authority on causation in the offence of causing death by driving while unlicensed, disqualified or uninsured. The Supreme Court held that mere involvement in the incident was insufficient; there must be at least some act or omission in the driving that contributed to the death.

### R v Kennedy (No 2)
**R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] UKHL 38; [2008] 1 AC 269**

A major causation case. The House of Lords held that where a fully informed and responsible adult self-administers a drug, that voluntary act breaks the chain of causation for unlawful act manslaughter against the supplier.

Though not limited to post-2006 law, it is one of the leading homicide/causation authorities of the modern period.

---

## I. Assisted suicide

### R (Purdy) v DPP
**R (Purdy) v Director of Public Prosecutions [2009] UKHL 45; [2010] 1 AC 345**

A landmark House of Lords case requiring the DPP to clarify the prosecution policy on assisted suicide under **Suicide Act 1961, s 2**.

### R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice
**R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice [2014] UKSC 38; [2015] AC 657**

A major constitutional and criminal law case on assisted suicide. The Supreme Court declined to declare the prohibition incompatible at that stage, but the judgments show deep judicial engagement with autonomy, dignity, and the limits of criminalisation.

### R (Conway) v Secretary of State for Justice
**[2018] EWCA Civ 1431; [2019] QB 839**
Further important authority on the same issue.

---

## J. Whole life orders and sentencing compatibility

### Vinter and others v United Kingdom
**Vinter v United Kingdom (2013) 63 EHRR 1, ECtHR (GC)**

Held that irreducible life sentences may violate **Article 3 ECHR** unless there is both a prospect of release and a possibility of review.

### R v McLoughlin; R v Newell
**[2014] EWCA Crim 188; [2014] 1 WLR 3964**

- هل توجد شروط وأحكام إلكترونية ملزمة؟

### عملياً:
العقود الإلكترونية في الإمارات **قابلة للنفاذ** من حيث المبدأ، بشرط استيفاء متطلبات القانون والإثبات.

## 5) **العمل**

القانون الأساسي هنا هو:

### **المرسوم بقانون اتحادي رقم 33 لسنة 2021 بشأن تنظيم علاقات العمل**
**Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 Regulating Labour Relations**

ولائحته التنفيذية:

### **قرار مجلس الوزراء رقم 1 لسنة 2022 بشأن اللائحة التنفيذية للمرسوم بقانون اتحادي رقم 33 لسنة 2021**

وفي 2023 استمرت تطبيقات هذا النظام وظهرت تحديثات وقرارات تنفيذية وتفسيرات قضائية مهمة.

### لماذا هو مهم في قانون العقود؟
لأن عقد العمل في الإمارات:
- يخضع لقواعد آمرة
- لا يجوز الاتفاق على ما ينتقص من الحقوق الدنيا للعامل
- أي شرط تعاقدي أقل من الحد القانوني قد يُهدر

### أهم الحقوق/المسائل:
- الأجر
- فترة التجربة
- عدم التمييز
- الإجازات
- إنهاء الخدمة
- الإنذار
- التعويض عن الفصل غير المشروع في بعض الصور
- الشرط الجزائي أو شرط عدم المنافسة ضمن الضوابط القانونية

### نقطة مهمة:
في عقود العمل، **القانون الحمائي** يتقدم غالباً على مبدأ حرية التعاقد.

# ثالثاً: قرارات المحكمة والمبادئ القضائية المهمة

في الإمارات، السوابق القضائية ليست ملزمة بنفس الشكل الموجود في بعض الأنظمة الأنجلوسكسونية، لكن **أحكام محكمة التمييز** و**المحكمة الاتحادية العليا** و**محكمة النقض/التمييز في دبي وأبوظبي** ذات قيمة إرشادية عالية جداً.

## مبادئ قضائية متكررة في منازعات العقود:
### 1) **حسن النية في التنفيذ**
استناداً إلى **المادة 246 من قانون المعاملات المدنية**  
المحاكم الإماراتية تؤكد باستمرار أن تنفيذ العقد لا يقتصر على نصوصه الحرفية، بل يشمل:
- مستلزماته
- ما يوجبه العرف
- طبيعة التعامل
- حسن النية

### 2) **تفسير العقود**
إذا كانت العبارة واضحة، لا يجوز الانحراف عنها.  
أما إذا وُجد غموض، فللمحكمة سلطة تفسير العقد وفق:
- نية المتعاقدين
- طبيعة المعاملة
- العرف
- حسن النية

### 3) **الشرط الجزائي**
المحاكم الإماراتية تقبل الشرط الجزائي، لكن يجوز لها تعديله إذا:
- كان مبالغاً فيه
- أو لم يقع ضرر يعادل المبلغ المتفق عليه

وهذا مبدأ مستقر في قانون المعاملات المدنية.

### 4) **القوة القاهرة والظروف الطارئة**
المحاكم تميز بين:
- **الاستحالة**: قد تؤدي إلى انقضاء الالتزام
- **الإرهاق الشديد دون استحالة**: قد تؤدي إلى تدخل القاضي لتعديل الالتزام وفق **المادة 249**

### 5) **العقود الإلكترونية والإثبات**
اتجهت المحاكم إلى قبول:
- الرسائل الإلكترونية
- المراسلات
- المستندات الرقمية
كوسائل إثبات، متى توفرت الموثوقية والنسبة إلى صاحبها.

# خامساً: ملاحظات مهمة بشأن القضايا والأحكام

## هل توجد “قضايا رئيسية” يجب معرفتها؟
نعم، لكن في الإمارات توجد مشكلة عملية وهي أن **نشر الأحكام ليس شاملاً دائماً** مثل بعض الولايات القضائية الأخرى، كما أن الوصول إلى جميع الأحكام الحديثة قد يكون عبر قواعد بيانات قانونية متخصصة.

لذلك، عند الحديث مع العميل، الأفضل التركيز على:
- **المبادئ القضائية المستقرة**
- وأحكام **المحكمة الاتحادية العليا**
- وأحكام **محكمة تمييز دبي** و**محكمة نقض أبوظبي** المنشورة أو المتاحة في قواعد البيانات القانونية

### من المبادئ القضائية المتكررة:
- لا يجوز الاتفاق على ما يخالف النصوص الآمرة في العمل أو الوكالات أو التأمينات
- حسن النية جزء من تنفيذ العقد
- المحكمة تملك تكييف العلاقة القانونية بحسب حقيقتها لا بحسب التسمية التي يضعها الأطراف
- الشرط الجزائي يخضع لرقابة القضاء
- الكتابة الإلكترونية والتوقيع الإلكتروني قد تكون لهما الحجية القانونية

إذا كان العميل لديه نزاع محدد، فالأفضل البحث في:
- أحكام **تمييز دبي** في العقود التجارية
- أحكام **المحكمة الاتحادية العليا** في الفسخ والتعويض وحسن النية
- أحكام العمل الصادرة بعد سريان **المرسوم بقانون 33 لسنة 2021**

For **contract law in England and Wales**, the key point is that there is **no single codifying “Contract Act”**. The law comes from a mix of **common law cases** and **specific statutes** affecting particular issues such as formation, unfair terms, misrepresentation, consumer rights, and formalities.

## 1. Core common law principles and leading cases

A client asking about “rights under contract law” should usually be advised on these core areas:

### A. Formation of contract
A valid contract generally requires **offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, and certainty of terms**.

Key cases:
- **Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co** [1893] 1 QB 256 (CA) — unilateral offers; objective intention to be bound.
- **Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd** [1953] 1 QB 401 (CA) — display of goods is usually an invitation to treat.
- **Fisher v Bell** [1961] 1 QB 394 (DC) — invitation to treat.
- **Entores Ltd v Miles Far East Corporation** [1955] 2 QB 327 (CA) — acceptance by instantaneous communications.
- **Brogden v Metropolitan Railway Co** (1877) 2 App Cas 666 (HL) — acceptance by conduct.
- **Currie v Misa** (1875) LR 10 Ex 153 — classic definition of consideration.
- **Thomas v Thomas** (1842) 2 QB 851 — consideration must have some value in the eyes of the law.
- **Balfour v Balfour** [1919] 2 KB 571 (CA) — no intention to create legal relations in domestic agreements.
- **Edwards v Skyways Ltd** [1964] 1 WLR 349 (QB) — presumption of intention in commercial agreements.

### B. Terms of the contract
Questions often arise as to whether a statement is a term, whether terms were incorporated, and how exclusion clauses operate.

Key cases:
- **Poussard v Spiers and Pond** (1876) 1 QBD 410 — condition vs warranty.
- **Bettini v Gye** (1876) 1 QBD 183 — warranty.
- **Hong Kong Fir Shipping Co Ltd v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd** [1962] 2 QB 26 (CA) — innominate terms.
- **L’Estrange v F Graucob Ltd** [1934] 2 KB 394 (CA) — signature usually binds.
- **Parker v South Eastern Railway Co** (1877) 2 CPD 416 — notice of terms.
- **Olley v Marlborough Court Ltd** [1949] 1 KB 532 (CA) — terms must be communicated before or at contracting.
- **Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking Ltd** [1971] 2 QB 163 (CA) — onerous terms require clear notice.
- **Interfoto Picture Library Ltd v Stiletto Visual Programmes Ltd** [1989] QB 433 (CA) — particularly onerous terms need special notice.

### C. Misrepresentation
If the client entered a contract because of false statements, misrepresentation law may apply.

Key authorities:
- **Misrepresentation Act 1967**, especially:
  - **s 2(1)** — damages for negligent misrepresentation.
  - **s 2(2)** — court discretion to award damages in lieu of rescission.
- **Derry v Peek** (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (HL) — fraudulent misrepresentation.
- **Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd** [1964] AC 465 (HL) — negligent misstatement.
- **Smith v Land & House Property Corp** (1884) 28 Ch D 7 (CA) — statements of opinion may be representations of fact.
- **Redgrave v Hurd** (1881) 20 Ch D 1 (CA) — claimant may rescind even if they could have discovered truth.
- **Leaf v International Galleries** [1950] 2 KB 86 (CA) — limits on rescission after lapse of time.

### D. Privity and third-party rights
Traditionally, only parties to a contract could sue on it, but statute now creates important exceptions.

Key authorities:
- **Tweddle v Atkinson** (1861) 1 B & S 393 — classic privity rule.
- **Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd** [1915] AC 847 (HL) — privity and consideration.
- **Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999**, especially:
  - **s 1** — third party may enforce a term if the contract expressly says so, or the term purports to confer a benefit on them.
  - **s 2** — variation/rescission restrictions once third-party rights crystallise.

### E. Breach and remedies
A client will usually want to know what remedies are available: damages, termination, specific performance, injunctions, restitution.

Key cases:
- **Robinson v Harman** (1848) 1 Ex 850 — expectation measure of damages.
- **Hadley v Baxendale** (1854) 9 Exch 341 — remoteness of damage.
- **Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd v Newman Industries Ltd** [1949] 2 KB 528 (CA) — remoteness.
- **The Heron II**: **Koufos v C Czarnikow Ltd** [1969] 1 AC 350 (HL) — remoteness.
- **British Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co Ltd v Underground Electric Railways Co of London Ltd** [1912] AC 673 (HL) — mitigation.
- **White & Carter (Councils) Ltd v McGregor** [1962] AC 413 (HL) — affirmation and debt claims.
- **Beswick v Beswick** [1968] AC 58 (HL) — specific performance.
- **Attorney General v Blake** [2001] 1 AC 268 (HL) — exceptional account of profits for breach of contract.
- **Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis** [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172 — penalty clauses and legitimate interest test.

### F. Frustration
If performance becomes impossible or radically different, frustration may discharge the contract.

Key authorities:
- **Taylor v Caldwell** (1863) 3 B & S 826 — destruction of subject matter.
- **Krell v Henry** [1903] 2 KB 740 (CA) — frustration of common purpose.
- **Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham Urban District Council** [1956] AC 696 (HL) — frustration is narrow.
- **Fibrosa Spolka Akcyjna v Fairbairn Lawson Combe Barbour Ltd** [1943] AC 32 (HL) — recovery of money after frustration.
- **Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943** — adjusts losses following frustration.

## 2. Key statutes in England and Wales contract law

### A. Consumer Rights Act 2015
This is one of the most important statutes if the client is a **consumer**.

Important parts:
- **Part 1, Chapter 2** — goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, and as described.
- **Part 1, Chapter 3** — digital content rights.
- **Part 1, Chapter 4** — services to be performed with reasonable care and skill.
- **Part 2** — unfair terms in consumer contracts.

Key case background on unfair terms:
- **Director General of Fair Trading v First National Bank plc** [2001] UKHL 52, [2002] 1 AC 481.
- **Office of Fair Trading v Abbey National plc** [2009] UKSC 6, [2010] 1 AC 696.
- **ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis** [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172.

### B. Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977
Important in business contracts and some consumer contexts (though much consumer unfair-terms law is now in the CRA 2015).

Key provisions:
- **s 2** — exclusion of liability for negligence.
- **s 3** — written standard terms.
- **s 6** and **s 7** — sale and hire-purchase related implied terms.
- **s 11** — reasonableness test.
- **Schedule 2** — guidelines for reasonableness.

Key cases:
- **Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd** [1980] AC 827 (HL) — exclusion clauses governed by construction and statute, not a rule of fundamental breach.
- **George Mitchell (Chesterhall) Ltd v Finney Lock Seeds Ltd** [1983] 2 AC 803 (HL) — reasonableness under UCTA.
- **Watford Electronics Ltd v Sanderson CFL Ltd** [2001] EWCA Civ 317, [2001] 1 All ER (Comm) 696 — negotiated commercial limitation clauses.

### C. Misrepresentation Act 1967
Already noted above; central where entry into the contract was induced by false statements.

### D. Sale of Goods Act 1979
Still highly relevant, especially for **business-to-business sale of goods** and in areas not replaced by the CRA for consumers.

Important provisions:
- **s 12** — title.
- **s 13** — sale by description.
- **s 14** — satisfactory quality and fitness for purpose.
- **s 15** — sale by sample.

Key cases:
- **Arcos Ltd v EA Ronaasen & Son** [1933] AC 470 (HL).
- **Re Moore & Co Ltd and Landauer & Co** [1921] 2 KB 519 (CA).
- **Grant v Australian Knitting Mills Ltd** [1936] AC 85 (PC) — persuasive/common law significance on merchantable quality.
- **Clegg v Andersson (t/a Nordic Marine)** [2003] EWCA Civ 320, [2003] 1 WLR 2120.

### E. Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982
Still important mainly for **business contracts** for services and transfer of goods in certain contexts.

Key provisions:
- **s 13** — reasonable care and skill in services.
- **s 14** — performance within reasonable time.
- **s 15** — reasonable charge.

### F. Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989
Important where the contract concerns land or guarantees.

Key provisions:
- **s 2** — contracts for sale or disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, incorporating all terms, and signed.
- **s 4** — guarantees to be evidenced in writing.

Key case:
- **Firstpost Homes Ltd v Johnson** [1995] 1 WLR 1567 (CA) — strict approach to s 2 formalities.

### G. Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998
Relevant for businesses claiming statutory interest on unpaid invoices in commercial contracts.

### H. Limitation Act 1980
Important for time limits:
- Usually **6 years** for simple contracts: **s 5**
- Usually **12 years** for deeds: **s 8**

- قرارات مجلس الوزراء المتعلقة بالأنشطة ذات الأثر الاستراتيجي.

### أ. في لوائح الشركات 2022
المبدأ الأساسي:

- ومسؤولية المساهم/الشريك محدودة بمقدار مساهمته، إلا في حالات استثنائية مثل:

- **Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2021**
- النصوص الخاصة بالـ LLC والشركات المساهمة ومسؤولية المديرين والمؤسسين.

For a client asking generally about **contract law in England and Wales**, the answer will depend heavily on the issue in dispute, but there are a number of **core statutes and leading cases** that commonly govern contractual rights. Since you specifically mention **“[2023] EWCA Civ 2104”**, I should note first that **EWCA Civ neutral citation numbers in 2023 did not run as high as 2104**. - a typo,

---

## 1. Core statutes in contract law

### A. Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s 2
This is crucial where the contract concerns the **sale or other disposition of an interest in land**.

- **Section 2** requires such contracts to:
  - be **in writing**,
  - incorporate **all expressly agreed terms** in one document or, where contracts are exchanged, in each,
  - and be **signed by or on behalf of each party**.

Failure to comply generally makes the contract **void**.

**Key case:**
- **Record v Bell [1991] 1 WLR 853 (CA)** — strict approach to s 2 formalities.

### B. Misrepresentation Act 1967
Important where a client says they were induced to contract by a false statement.

Key provisions:
- **s 2(1)**: creates a statutory claim for damages for negligent misrepresentation unless the representor proves they had reasonable grounds to believe the statement was true.
- **s 2(2)**: gives the court discretion to award damages in lieu of rescission.
- **s 3**: controls attempts to exclude liability for misrepresentation, now read alongside the fairness regime under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and formerly UCTA.

**Key cases:**
- **Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297 (CA)** — damages under s 2(1) are assessed on the tortious basis, broadly akin to deceit.
- **William Sindall plc v Cambridgeshire County Council [1994] 1 WLR 1016 (CA)** — rescission, affirmation, and damages in lieu.
- **Salt v Stratstone Specialist Ltd [2015] EWCA Civ 745** — rescission for misrepresentation.

### C. Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977
Still very important in **business-to-business contracts** and some non-consumer settings, especially for exclusion and limitation clauses.

Key points:
- **s 2**: exclusion of liability for death/personal injury caused by negligence is void; other negligence exclusions must satisfy **reasonableness**.
- **s 3**: where one party deals on the other’s written standard terms, exclusions/limitations may be subject to reasonableness.
- **s 11** and **Schedule 2**: reasonableness test.

**Key cases:**
- **Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd [1980] AC 827 (HL)** — exclusion clauses are a matter of construction, controlled by statute rather than a separate doctrine of fundamental breach.
- **Watford Electronics Ltd v Sanderson CFL Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 317, [2001] 1 All ER (Comm) 696** — reasonableness in negotiated commercial contracts between experienced parties.
- **St Albans City and District Council v International Computers Ltd [1996] 4 All ER 481 (CA)** — limitation clause failed reasonableness.

### D. Consumer Rights Act 2015
This is the central statute where the client is a **consumer** contracting with a **trader**.

Key parts:
- **Part 1, Chapter 2**: contracts for goods.
- **Chapter 3**: digital content.
- **Chapter 4**: services.
- **Part 2**: unfair terms.

Important rights include:
- goods must be of **satisfactory quality**, **fit for purpose**, and **as described**;
- services must be performed with **reasonable care and skill**;
- unfair terms are **not binding** on consumers.

**Key cases / authorities:**
Because the CRA 2015 consolidated earlier law, many older authorities remain influential conceptually:
- **Director General of Fair Trading v First National Bank plc [2001] UKHL 52, [2002] 1 AC 481** — fairness assessment of consumer terms.
- **ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172** — penalty doctrine and consumer fairness under the predecessor regulations; still highly important under CRA unfair-terms analysis.

### E. Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998
Relevant for businesses claiming:
- statutory interest,
- fixed compensation,
- and sometimes reasonable debt recovery costs
on overdue commercial invoices.

### F. Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999
Important where someone who is not a party to the contract seeks to enforce a term.

- A third party may enforce a term if:
  - the contract expressly says so, or
  - the term purports to confer a benefit on them, unless on proper construction the parties did not intend that.

**Key case:**
- **Nisshin Shipping Co Ltd v Cleaves & Co Ltd [2003] EWHC 2602 (Comm), [2004] 1 Lloyd’s Rep 38**.

### G. Limitation Act 1980
Critical for whether a claim is still in time.

Typical periods:
- **6 years** for simple contract claims: **s 5**
- **12 years** for deeds: **s 8**

Accrual issues can be complex, especially in indemnities, guarantees, and latent damage contexts.

## 2. Key common law principles and leading cases

## A. Formation of contract

### Offer and acceptance
- **Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256 (CA)** — unilateral offers and acceptance by performance.
- **Entores Ltd v Miles Far East Corporation [1955] 2 QB 327 (CA)** — acceptance by instantaneous communication.
- **RTS Flexible Systems Ltd v Molkerei Alois Müller GmbH & Co KG [2010] UKSC 14, [2010] 1 WLR 753** — whether a contract exists depends on objective intention and whether essential terms are agreed.

### Consideration
- **Currie v Misa (1875) LR 10 Ex 153** — classic definition.
- **Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605 (HL)** — part payment of a debt is not good consideration for discharge of the whole, subject to exceptions.
- **MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd [2018] UKSC 24, [2019] AC 119** — no oral modification clauses; discussion of practical benefit and consideration.

### Intention to create legal relations
- **Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571 (CA)** — domestic arrangements usually not intended to be legally binding.
- **Edwards v Skyways Ltd [1964] 1 WLR 349 (QB)** — commercial agreements presumed intended to create legal relations.

---

## B. Terms of the contract

### Express terms and incorporation
- **L'Estrange v F Graucob Ltd [1934] 2 KB 394 (CA)** — signature generally binds a party to contractual terms.
- **Parker v South Eastern Railway Co (1877) 2 CPD 416 (CA)** — reasonable notice of terms.
- **Interfoto Picture Library Ltd v Stiletto Visual Programmes Ltd [1989] QB 433 (CA)** — particularly onerous or unusual terms require especially clear notice.

### Implied terms
- **The Moorcock (1889) 14 PD 64 (CA)** — business efficacy.
- **Shirlaw v Southern Foundries (1926) Ltd [1939] 2 KB 206 (CA)** — “officious bystander” test.
- **Marks and Spencer plc v BNP Paribas Securities Services Trust Co (Jersey) Ltd [2015] UKSC 72, [2016] AC 742** — modern restatement: implication of terms is not a free-standing test of reasonableness; necessity is central.

### Entire agreement / no oral modification
- **MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd [2018] UKSC 24, [2019] AC 119** — no oral modification clauses generally effective.
- **First Tower Trustees Ltd v CDS (Superstores International) Ltd [2018] EWCA Civ 1396, [2019] 1 WLR 637** — non-reliance clauses can amount to exclusion clauses and be subject to reasonableness controls.

---

## C. Interpretation of contracts

Modern English contract law places major emphasis on **objective interpretation**.

Key authorities:
- **Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896 (HL)** — foundational principles of interpretation.
- **Chartbrook Ltd v Persimmon Homes Ltd [2009] UKHL 38, [2009] AC 1101** — interpretation and exclusion of prior negotiations.
- **Rainy Sky SA v Kookmin Bank [2011] UKSC 50, [2011] 1 WLR 2900** — where there are two possible constructions, the court may prefer the one more consistent with business common sense.
- **Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36, [2015] AC 1619** — business common sense cannot undervalue the natural meaning of the words.
- **Wood v Capita Insurance Services Ltd [2017] UKSC 24, [2017] AC 1173** — textualism and contextualism are not conflicting paradigms; interpretation is a unitary exercise.
- **Sara & Hossein Asset Holdings Ltd v Blacks Outdoor Retail Ltd [2023] UKSC 2, [2023] AC 1258** — interpretation of service charge clauses and the relevance of commercial consequences.

---

## D. Misrepresentation, mistake, duress, undue influence

### Misrepresentation
Already noted under the 1967 Act, but also:
- **Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (HL)** — fraudulent misrepresentation.
- **Redgrave v Hurd (1881) 20 Ch D 1 (CA)** — representee can rely even if they could have discovered the truth.
- **Spice Girls Ltd v Aprilia World Service BV [2002] EWCA Civ 15, [2002] EMLR 27** — representation by conduct.

### Mistake
- **Bell v Lever Bros Ltd [1932] AC 161 (HL)** — common mistake at common law.
- **Great Peace Shipping Ltd v Tsavliris Salvage (International) Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 1407, [2003] QB 679** — leading modern authority; no separate equitable doctrine of common mistake surviving in that form.

### Duress
- **Universe Tankships Inc of Monrovia v International Transport Workers Federation [1983] 1 AC 366 (HL)** — economic duress principles.
- **DSND Subsea Ltd v Petroleum Geo Services ASA [2000] BLR 530 (EWHC (TCC))** — practical formulation of economic duress.
- **Times Travel (UK) Ltd v Pakistan International Airlines Corp [2021] UKSC 40, [2022] AC 1315** — lawful act duress is narrow.

### Undue influence
Often relevant where guarantees or family transactions are involved:
- **Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No 2) [2001] UKHL 44, [2002] 2 AC 773** — leading authority.
